blocks.p: This was around the time I had just finished my A/Ls.
Berserk was technically one of my first proper steps into anime, although I did not continue watching anime seriously afterward. I watched it, respected it, and then basically disappeared again.
But looking back, it planted something.

Guts was completely different from the kinds of protagonists I was used to. His life is brutal, unfair, psychologically exhausting, and sometimes it genuinely feels like the universe itself is against him. Yet he continues moving.
That idea stayed with me:

blocks.q: You do not need an easy life to keep moving forward.

blocks.p: Then came One Piece.
This is where my anime journey actually exploded.
I started around July 2024 and somehow finished the available story in roughly three months. Looking back, my only regret is that I watched it too fast. I was basically inhaling episodes. 💀
And after finishing it, I had a problem:
Nothing felt the same.

It became difficult to immediately attach myself to another story because One Piece had given me such a massive world, such a huge cast, so much history, so many emotional payoffs, and a main character who slowly changed the way I looked at life.
At first, I actually found one thing about Luffy annoying.
He kept loudly repeating his dream.

blocks.q: I'm going to become King of the Pirates.

blocks.p: I remember thinking: Who announces their impossible dream this confidently? Is this guy dumb?
Turns out, I was the one thinking inside a cage.
Luffy made me realize that there is nothing embarrassing about having a huge dream. The embarrassing part is abandoning your dream because other people might laugh at it.
He does not constantly reshape himself to please the world. He knows what matters to him: his dream, his freedom, and his people.
That simplicity is powerful.

I used to overthink things before acting. Luffy's way of moving through life made me think more about enjoying the process, trusting myself, and dealing with problems when they actually arrive instead of mentally fighting twenty imaginary futures.

blocks.q: Dream loudly. Protect your people. Keep moving.

blocks.p: That is probably the simplest way I can describe what Luffy gave me.

blocks.h: One Piece did not just give me one character

blocks.p: It gave me an entire collection of people who affected different parts of me:
One Piece was the first anime that stopped being "a show I liked" and became something closer to a place I return to.
After One Piece, I started exploring properly.
Attack on Titan came next around November to December 2024, followed by Jujutsu Kaisen, then Demon Slayer around January to February 2025.
This era taught me something important about my own taste:
I do not automatically love an anime because it is popular, beautifully animated, or technically impressive.
I need the story to make me feel something.

That is why I can appreciate the insane animation of Demon Slayer or JJK while still not putting them near One Piece emotionally. And it is why I can love a flawed or strange character if their struggle feels real.
This period was basically me discovering my personal anime filter.

blocks.q: Pretty animation can get my attention. Emotion is what makes me stay.

blocks.p: My second One Piece watch was different.
This time, I watched it with my sister.

That instantly changed the experience because now I was not only revisiting scenes I loved. I was waiting for someone else to reach them. I knew the emotional landmines ahead and had to sit there pretending to be normal. 😂
The second watch also made me appreciate how much setup, character writing, foreshadowing, and emotional detail I had blasted past during my first three-month speedrun.
One Piece started becoming part of my family life too, not just my personal watch history.
In early 2026 I watched Black Clover again, this time with my sister.
Asta is one of those characters whose entire existence is basically a refusal to accept the limits given to him.
He is loud. Very loud. 😭
But underneath that is something I genuinely respect: work until the impossible becomes less impossible.
This was also around the time I watched Solo Leveling and continued jumping across different genres and styles.
By this point anime was not a phase anymore. It had become one of my main forms of entertainment.

stops.name: "Why Is This School Anime So Good?"
stops.title: Classroom of the Elite

blocks.p: I never expected a high-school anime to become one of my favorites.
From the outside, Classroom of the Elite looked like exactly the kind of thing I would probably ignore.
Then I met Ayanokoji.

What fascinated me was not simply that he is intelligent or capable. It was his awareness, emotional control, observation, ability to handle complicated situations, and discipline about what he reveals.
He also made me think about qualities I want to improve in myself: staying composed, reading situations better, knowing when to speak, and not reacting emotionally to everything.

There are absolutely parts of him I do not want to copy, especially the way he reduces people to tools. But that actually makes him more interesting to me, because learning from a character does not mean agreeing with everything they do.

blocks.q: Take the discipline. Leave the dehumanization.

blocks.p: That is my Ayanokoji rule. 😂
Then Re:Zero happened.
At first I was not impressed.
Subaru looked like a dumb simp. The opening felt slow. I was basically preparing to judge the whole thing too early.
Then around episode 6, the story grabbed me by the collar and refused to let go.
One minute Re:Zero can feel warm, funny, or almost cozy. Then everything collapses.
And what changed my opinion on Subaru is that Return by Death is not really a cool superpower. It is a curse disguised as a mechanic.

He can be killed horribly, watch people he loves die, completely break mentally, wake up again, and then walk into the same room pretending everything is fine because nobody else remembers what happened.
That loneliness is insane.
I originally saw his emotional behavior as weakness. Eventually I realized those same traits are why he becomes so attached to people and why he keeps throwing himself back into hell for them.
His suffering is immeasurable, but somehow he still keeps choosing another attempt.
Re:Zero reminded me that courage is not always looking fearless.
Sometimes courage is being completely destroyed and still saying:
It is now one of the best anime I have ever watched, and one of the biggest surprises of my entire journey.

stops.name: Wait... I Like Romance Anime Now?
stops.title: The Fragrant Flower Blooms with Dignity

blocks.p: This was another genre I never expected to care about.
The Fragrant Flower Blooms with Dignity became my first proper romance anime, and instead of feeling like a collection of forced anime romance tropes, it felt sincere.

What I liked was the maturity of the relationship, the emotional honesty, and the feeling that these were two people genuinely growing closer instead of a story endlessly delaying everything for cheap tension.
I liked it enough that after finishing the anime, I started reading the manga to continue the story.
That was another important point in the journey:

blocks.q: I stopped choosing anime based on what I thought I was "supposed" to like.

blocks.p: If the story is good, the genre does not matter.

stops.name: Stories I Never Would Have Tried Before

blocks.p: By this stage I had gone from rejecting anime as a whole to watching psychological thrillers, fantasy, isekai, romance, action, school dramas, slice-of-life stories, dark fantasy, comedy, and manga adaptations I would have completely ignored a few years earlier.
Shows like Mushoku Tensei, Smoking Behind the Supermarket with You, Frieren, Mob Psycho 100, Chainsaw Man, Hell's Paradise, and others kept widening that range.
That is probably one of the coolest things anime gave me outside the stories themselves:

blocks.h: made me more willing to try things before judging them.

blocks.p: Which is hilarious considering this entire journey started because I judged anime before trying it.
Perfect full-circle punishment. 💀

save: MAIN QUEST: Become a better version of myself

moments.title: Luffy puts the straw hat on Nami

text.p: That feeling was crazy. This was one of the early moments where One Piece showed me what kind of protagonist Luffy really is. He does not need a giant speech. He understands what Nami is asking for, gives her his most precious possession, and walks toward the fight.
Sanji somehow managed to get hit by the backstory truck twice. His relationship with food, hunger, Zeff, rejection, and family made his personality hit very differently afterward.
A promise surviving across decades is exactly the kind of One Piece idea that sounds almost silly until the story absolutely destroys you with it.

moments.title: Robin says she wants to live

text.p: This is one of the scenes that affected me the most in all of anime.
Robin spent years believing her existence itself was a problem. She ran, hid, lost people, and eventually became so afraid of hurting the Straw Hats that she was willing to disappear for them.
Then Luffy basically tells the entire World Government: No. She is ours. We are coming to get her.
And Robin finally allows herself to want something again.
Even after multiple rewatches, that scene still hits me.

moments.title: Every time Luffy declares his dream

text.p: It used to annoy me.
Now it reminds me why I love him.
No speech. No request for praise. Just loyalty pushed to an absurd level.
Watching Luffy finally reach Ace, actually free him, and then lose him anyway is brutal. What destroys the scene even more is seeing Luffy completely collapse afterward.
Luffy's attitude in Wano perfectly captures why I love him. As long as he is still alive, the fight is not automatically over.
This is probably my favorite One Piece clip of all time.
The animation, the drums, Luffy remembering the people of Wano, the exhaustion, Kaido warning him that continuing could kill him, and Luffy basically responding with zero fear.
Even thinking about that scene still gives me chills.
The running sequence broke me.
Kuma's story is one of those pieces of fiction where you already know the character survived enormous pain, but once the full weight of it is shown, everything about him changes.
Even remembering that sequence can make my eyes wet.
The references to the Sun God and the idea that "they will surely meet" gave me that specific One Piece feeling where lore, mystery, destiny, and emotion suddenly collide.
I do not even fully understand why this song gets me so badly.
Sometimes the opening seconds are enough.
It feels connected to the entire journey of One Piece now, not just an ending theme. If they ever use it near the actual ending of the story, I am finished. 😭
That was one of the first moments where the show made it clear that it was willing to become much darker than I expected.
Watching everything go wrong so completely made the "reset" mechanic stop feeling safe.
A lot of his deaths are stuck in my memory because the physical pain is only half of it. He has to return carrying memories that the people around him do not have.
That is what makes Re:Zero terrifying.
